conversation.content: Let's design a real-time chat system for 1:1 and group messaging. What questions do you have before we start?

Sure. What's the scale — how many users and messages per day? Do we need to support media messages or just text? What about message history — how far back should users be able to scroll? And what platforms — web, iOS, Android?
100M DAU, 1 billion messages per day. Text only for now. Full message history — users can scroll back forever. All three platforms. Go ahead and start with the high-level architecture.

Okay so there are a bunch of components. There's the thing that handles the WebSocket connections from clients. And then there's the part that routes messages between users. And then we need to store the messages somewhere. And there's the piece that tracks who's online. And we need push notifications for when people are offline. So basically the message comes in from the sender, goes through the routing thing, gets stored, and then gets sent out to the recipient if they're connected, or a push notification goes out if they're not.
Can you draw the high-level architecture? Show me the components and how they connect.

Draw it... okay, um. So you've got the clients on the left. And they connect to... the WebSocket servers. And the WebSocket servers talk to... the message service. Which talks to the database. And also to... there's the thing that figures out which server the other person is on. And push notifications come from... somewhere in here. I'm having trouble organizing this visually. Let me try describing it more clearly. There are five main services...
Let me help structure this. Start by listing the components as boxes, then draw the arrows showing data flow. Take a moment to think about it before explaining.

Okay, let me organize. Components: 1) API Gateway / Load Balancer. 2) WebSocket Gateway — manages persistent connections. 3) Message Service — handles message creation, routing logic. 4) Session Registry — tracks which WebSocket gateway each user is connected to, in Redis. 5) Message Store — persistent database for all messages. 6) Notification Service — sends push notifications for offline users. Flow: Client connects to WebSocket Gateway via the Load Balancer. When sending a message, it goes: Client -> WebSocket Gateway -> Message Service -> Message Store (persist) and simultaneously -> Session Registry (lookup recipient) -> recipient's WebSocket Gateway -> recipient's Client. If recipient is offline: Message Service -> Notification Service -> APNs/FCM.
Better. Now let's dig into the WebSocket Gateway. How do you handle 100M concurrent connections?

So each WebSocket connection takes some memory — roughly 10-50 KB per connection depending on buffer sizes. If each gateway server handles 50,000 connections, we need 2,000 servers for 100M connections. That's a big fleet. When a user connects, the gateway registers the mapping (user_id -> gateway_server_id) in Redis. For connection health, the client sends periodic heartbeats — if the server doesn't receive a heartbeat within 30 seconds, it closes the connection and removes the registry entry.
How does the Message Service route a message to the right gateway?

The Message Service looks up the recipient's user_id in the Session Registry (Redis). It gets back the gateway_server_id where that user is connected. Then it needs to forward the message to that specific gateway. For inter-service communication, I'd use... let me think. Direct gRPC call from Message Service to the target Gateway? Or a pub/sub channel? With 2,000 gateway servers, direct gRPC means the Message Service needs connections to potentially all of them. That's manageable — connection pooling handles it. Alternatively, each gateway subscribes to a Redis pub/sub channel named after itself. The Message Service publishes to the right channel. I prefer the pub/sub approach — it's more decoupled.
Tell me about the message storage. What database and schema?

1 billion messages per day. At maybe 300 bytes per message, that's 300 GB per day, 110 TB per year. For the access pattern — we read messages by conversation, ordered by time, with pagination. This is a classic Cassandra use case. Partition key: conversation_id. Clustering key: message_id (which is a time-based UUID, Snowflake-style, so it's naturally ordered). Columns: sender_id, content, created_at, status (sent, delivered, read). For group chats, same schema — the conversation_id represents the group. For the unbounded partition problem — a very active group chat could have millions of messages — I'd bucket by week or month: partition key becomes (conversation_id, time_bucket).
How do you handle group message delivery? A group has 500 members.

For a group message, the sender sends one message to the Message Service. The Message Service: 1) Persists the message once to the Message Store under the group's conversation_id. 2) Looks up all 500 members of the group from a Group Membership table. 3) For each member, checks the Session Registry for online status. 4) For online members, routes the message to their respective WebSocket Gateways. 5) For offline members, queues a push notification. Step 4 is a fan-out — 500 lookups and potentially 500 message deliveries. For very large groups (10K+ members), we'd batch the fan-out asynchronously through a queue.
What about message ordering? How do you guarantee messages appear in the correct order?

So ordering is per-conversation. The Message Service assigns each message a monotonically increasing sequence number per conversation. It's stored alongside the time-based ID. The client displays messages sorted by sequence number. For 1:1 chats, there's very little contention — messages alternate between two users. For group chats, concurrent messages from different senders need a serialization point. The sequence number generator could be a Redis INCR per conversation_id. For high-traffic groups, this Redis key could become a hot key — but even busy groups rarely exceed a few messages per second, so INCR's throughput is more than sufficient.
What failure scenarios concern you most in this design?

The scariest failure is the Session Registry (Redis) going down. Without it, we can't route messages to the right gateway. Mitigation: Redis Cluster with replicas. But if the whole cluster is down, we fall back to... hmm, we could have each gateway periodically write its connection list to a local file and serve it via an API. Other gateways could query all gateways to find a user — O(N) but it works as a last resort. Second concern: Cassandra write failures. If we can't persist a message, we must not acknowledge it to the sender. The client retries. We use an idempotency key per message to prevent duplicates.
How does the client know a message was delivered and read?

Delivery and read receipts are separate flows. When the recipient's client receives a message, it sends back a 'delivered' acknowledgment to the server, which updates the message status and notifies the sender. Similarly, when the recipient actually opens the conversation and views the message, the client sends a 'read' acknowledgment. These are lightweight messages on the same WebSocket. For group chats, delivery/read receipts per member get expensive — 500 receipts per message. We'd aggregate them: 'delivered to 498 of 500 members' rather than individual receipts, updated periodically.

We're almost done. Looking back, your verbal descriptions were detailed but hard to follow. In a real whiteboard interview, being able to draw clear diagrams and reference them makes communication much easier. How would you improve your presentation?

You're right — I tend to think in words rather than pictures. I should have started with a clean diagram: boxes for each service, arrows for data flow, and labeled the key data paths (send message, receive message, offline notification). Then I could reference the diagram: 'this arrow here handles X.' I also should have used a sequence diagram for the message flow — sender, gateway, service, store, gateway, receiver — instead of describing it as a numbered list. I'll practice diagramming before my next interview.

Good self-awareness. Your technical knowledge is solid — the Cassandra schema, group fan-out, and ordering logic were well thought out. But you struggled to organize your thoughts visually, which made the first 10 minutes of the interview harder to follow than they needed to be. Clear diagrams aren't just nice-to-have — they demonstrate architectural thinking. Thanks.

strengths: Strong Cassandra schema with time bucketing for unbounded partitions
Good message ordering approach with per-conversation sequence numbers
Practical group receipt aggregation to avoid fan-out explosion
weaknesses: Unable to organize thoughts visually — struggled when asked to draw architecture
Initial high-level description was vague and used imprecise language ('the thing', 'somewhere')
Communication was verbose and hard to follow without visual anchors
No API design discussion — what do the client-facing endpoints look like?
Failure handling was surface-level — didn't consider split-brain or network partition scenarios
